blocks.text: A. Secondary Open-Angle Mechanisms

items: **Mechanical Trabecular Obstruction:** Breakdown of the blood–aqueous barrier floods the anterior chamber with **plasmoid aqueous** rich in high-molecular-weight serum proteins, fibrin, inflammatory leukocytes, macrophages, and cellular debris that physically clog the intertrabecular spaces [1][2].

**Direct Trabeculitis:** Acute inflammatory infiltration and edema of the trabecular lamellae narrow intertrabecular pores and impair endothelial phagocytosis, classically seen in **herpetic (HSV, VZV, CMV) anterior uveitis**, Posner–Schlossman syndrome, and sarcoidosis [1][2].

**Chronic Trabecular Scarring & Endothelialization:** Recurrent or prolonged inflammation causes irreversible trabecular endothelial loss, extracellular matrix hyalinization, collapse of Schlemm's canal, and overgrowth of a fibrovascular or cuticular membrane over the meshwork [2].

**Corticosteroid-Induced Ocular Hypertension:** Topical, periocular, intravitreal, or systemic steroids—essential to control uveitis—induce myocilin expression, glycosaminoglycan accumulation, and decreased matrix metalloproteinase activity in the trabecular meshwork, causing steroid-induced IOP elevation in ~30–40% of normal individuals and an even higher proportion of chronic uveitis and pediatric patients [1][2].

blocks.text: B. Secondary Angle-Closure Mechanisms

items: **Pupillary Block Angle Closure (Iris Bombé):** Fibrinous inflammation creates **360° posterior synechiae (seclusio pupillae)** or a complete pupillary membrane (**occlusio pupillae**), blocking aqueous flow from the posterior to the anterior chamber; rising posterior chamber pressure bows the peripheral iris sharply forward (**iris bombé**), closing the angle [1][2].

**Non-Pupillary Block (Anterior Pulling) Angle Closure:** Organization and contraction of inflammatory exudates, keratic precipitates, or fibrovascular tissue within the angle recess pulls the peripheral iris onto the trabecular meshwork, generating broad-based or **tent-shaped peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS)** (typically densest inferiorly due to gravitational settling of cells) [2].

**Posterior Pushing (Ciliochoroidal Effusion) Angle Closure:** Severe inflammation of the ciliary body and choroid—classic in **Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (VKH) syndrome**, posterior scleritis, and sympathetic ophthalmia—produces annular supraciliary effusion with anterior rotation of the ciliary body and forward shift of the lens–iris diaphragm, inducing bilateral acute angle closure *without* pupillary block [2][3].

sections.heading: 3. Specific Uveitic Syndromes Strongly Associated with Glaucoma

rows: Unilateral (~90%), chronic low-grade anterior uveitis; diffuse **stellate KPs**, iris stromal atrophy/heterochromia, **no posterior synechiae**, fine bridging angle vessels (**Amsler sign** bleeding on paracentesis), cataract [3]

Chronic **open-angle glaucoma** (~15–60%) from trabecular sclerosis/rubeosis; **poor response to steroids** (avoid chronic unnecessary steroid escalation); frequently requires filtration or GDD [2][3]

Young–middle-aged adults; recurrent unilateral acute spikes (**IOP 40–60 mmHg**) with **disproportionately mild symptoms**, few fine white KPs, mild AC cells, open angle, slight mydriasis; strongly linked to **CMV** [2][3]

Acute **viral trabeculitis** + prostaglandin surge; episodes self-resolve in days–weeks with topical steroids, aqueous suppressants, and oral/topical valganciclovir (if CMV+); **~25%** develop chronic glaucomatous damage [2][3]
Unilateral **hypertensive uveitis**; **sectoral (HSV/VZV) or patchy (CMV) iris atrophy**, reduced corneal sensation (HSV/VZV), coin-shaped/linear KPs and endothelial cell loss (CMV) [3]

Acute severe **trabeculitis** and secondary open-angle (or synechial) glaucoma; requires **systemic/topical antivirals** (acyclovir/valacyclovir or valganciclovir) alongside steroids and aqueous suppressants [2][3]
Bilateral chronic **asymptomatic ('white-eye')** anterior uveitis in oligoarticular ANA-positive young girls; classic triad of **band keratopathy, cataract, and glaucoma** [3]

Open-angle trabecular scarring, PAS, pupillary block, and **marked pediatric steroid response** (glaucoma in 20–40%); aggressive scarring impairs trabeculectomy → **GDD or angle surgery (goniotomy/GATT)** preferred [2][4]
Acute recurrent unilateral alternating **fibrinous/hypopyon** iridocyclitis (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, IBD, psoriatic arthritis) [3]
Initial hypotony followed by acute IOP spikes from **fibrin clogging, 360° posterior synechiae/iris bombé**, or steroid response; aggressive cycloplegia prevents seclusio pupillae [2][3]
Bilateral **granulomatous** uveitis with mutton-fat KPs, Koeppe/Busacca iris nodules, **tent-shaped PAS**, and trabecular inflammatory nodules [3]
Mixed **trabecular granulomatous infiltration**, broad PAS, and steroid response; high prevalence of secondary glaucoma requiring IMT and filtering/GDD surgery [2][3]
Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis, serous retinal detachments, Sunset-glow fundus, Dalen–Fuchs nodules, auditory/integumentary signs [3]
Acute **bilateral non-pupillary-block angle closure** from annular ciliochoroidal effusion (unresponsive to LPI; responds to systemic steroids + cycloplegics); late PAS and steroid glaucoma [2][3]

sections.heading: 4. Differentiating Active Inflammatory IOP Rise vs. Steroid Response

blocks.text: A pivotal clinical challenge in uveitic glaucoma is distinguishing IOP elevation driven by **inadequately controlled inflammation** (trabeculitis/clogging) from **corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension**, as the therapeutic actions are diametrically opposite [1][4].

blocks.title: Clinical Differentiation Strategy
items: **Active Inflammatory IOP Rise:** Typically coincides with active anterior chamber cells/flare, fresh KPs, or worsening ocular congestion (e.g., acute herpetic trabeculitis or HLA-B27 flare). Management requires **intensifying topical/systemic anti-inflammatory therapy** (plus targeted antivirals if infectious) alongside aqueous suppressants [1][4].

**Corticosteroid-Induced OHT/Glaucoma:** Classically develops **2–6 weeks** after initiating or escalating potent corticosteroids (prednisolone acetate, dexamethasone, difluprednate, periocular/intravitreal implants) *after* anterior chamber inflammation has quieted. Management involves **tapering steroids**, switching to lower-IOP-risk agents (**loteprednol etabonate** or **fluorometholone**), or introducing early **steroid-sparing immunomodulatory therapy (IMT)** (methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, or anti-TNF biologics like adalimumab) [1][4].

sections.heading: 5. Principles of Medical, Laser & Surgical Management

blocks.text: A. Control of Inflammation & Medical IOP-Lowering Therapy

The foundational rule of uveitic glaucoma management is **simultaneous aggressive control of both intraocular inflammation and IOP** [1][4]. Always exclude infectious etiologies (HSV, VZV, CMV, syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis) before escalating immunosuppression, and prescribe **cycloplegics** (homatropine, cyclopentolate, or atropine) during active anterior uveitis to prevent posterior synechiae and relieve ciliary spasm [1][4].

items: **First-Line IOP Agents:** **Topical β-blockers** (timolol), **topical/oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors** (dorzolamide, brinzolamide, acetazolamide—which offer the added benefit of reducing uveitic cystoid macular edema), and **α₂-agonists** (brimonidine—monitoring for delayed granulomatous anterior uveitis hypersensitivity) [1][4].

**Agents Requiring Caution:** **Prostaglandin analogues (PGAs)** may rarely exacerbate anterior uveitis, induce **cystoid macular edema (CME)**, or reactivate **herpetic keratitis**; they are generally avoided during active inflammation or herpetic disease but can be cautiously added in quiet, non-herpetic eyes without CME if first-line agents are insufficient [1][4].

**Strictly Contraindicated Agents:** **Miotics (pilocarpine)** break down the blood–aqueous barrier, exacerbate anterior chamber inflammation, worsen ciliary pain, and strongly promote **posterior synechiae and seclusio pupillae** [1][4].

blocks.text: B. Laser and Surgical Interventions

items: **Nd:YAG Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI):** Indicated for **pupillary block / iris bombé**; because fibrin frequently occludes standard iridotomies (closure rate up to 50–60%), create **larger or multiple iridotomies** under intensive topical steroid coverage, proceeding to **surgical peripheral iridectomy** if recurrent closure occurs [4]. LPI is ineffective for VKH ciliochoroidal effusion [2].

**Laser Trabeculoplasty (ALT/SLT):** Generally **contraindicated** in active uveitic glaucoma due to risk of severe inflammatory rebound, acute IOP spikes, and accelerated PAS formation (limited use only in quiet steroid-induced OHT) [4].

**Perioperative Quiescence:** Whenever clinically feasible, achieve **at least 3 months of complete inflammatory quiescence** prior to elective incisional surgery and administer perioperative systemic/topical corticosteroid prophylaxis [4].

**Trabeculectomy with Antimetabolites (MMC/5-FU):** Mandatory antimetabolite modulation counters exuberant subconjunctival fibrosis, though long-term failure rates remain elevated (especially in young patients, JIA, and active uveitis) and early hypotony must be avoided [4].

**Glaucoma Drainage Devices (GDDs — Ahmed, Baerveldt, Aurolab AADI, Paul):** Widely considered the **preferred primary surgical intervention** in chronic/active uveitic glaucoma, JIA, pseudophakic/aphakic eyes, and prior failed filtration; **valved devices (Ahmed)** reduce postoperative hypotony in eyes with compromised ciliary body secretion [4].

**Angle Surgery & Cyclodestruction:** **Goniotomy, trabeculotomy, or GATT** achieves high success in pediatric **JIA uveitic glaucoma** with open angles [4]. **Transscleral cyclophotocoagulation (TSCPC / Micropulse CPC)** is reserved for refractory or low-vision eyes due to heightened risk of **chronic hypotony, phthisis bulbi**, and severe inflammatory flares [4].

Topical or oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., dorzolamide, acetazolamide)
Parasympathomimetic miotics (e.g., pilocarpine)
Selective α₂-adrenergic agonists (e.g., brimonidine)

What is the diagnosis and expected response to chronic topical corticosteroid therapy?

Posner–Schlossman syndrome; rapid complete normalization of IOP with steroids alone
HLA-B27 anterior uveitis; prompt resolution with intensive prednisolone and atropine
Sarcoidosis; resolution of tent-shaped PAS following periocular triamcinolone

sections.heading: 1. Diagnostic Accuracy: Sensitivity, Specificity, Predictive Values & ROC Curves

blocks.text: **Diagnostic accuracy** quantifies how reliably an index test (such as IOP measurement, OCT RNFL thickness, or frequency-doubling perimetry) classifies patients with and without disease relative to an established **reference gold standard** (e.g., confirmed glaucomatous optic neuropathy with reproducible visual field loss) [1][2]. Every binary diagnostic test produces a **2×2 contingency table** comprising **True Positives (TP)**, **False Positives (FP)**, **False Negatives (FN)**, and **True Negatives (TN)** [2].

Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN)   |   Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)
PPV = TP / (TP + FP)   |   NPV = TN / (TN + FN)
LR+ = Sensitivity / (1 − Specificity)   |   LR− = (1 − Sensitivity) / Specificity

items: **Sensitivity (True Positive Rate):** Proportion of truly diseased individuals correctly identified as positive; a test with very high sensitivity has few false negatives and reliably **rules out** disease when negative (**SnNout**) [2].

**Specificity (True Negative Rate):** Proportion of truly healthy individuals correctly identified as negative; a test with very high specificity has few false positives and reliably **rules in** disease when positive (**SpPin**) [2]. Both sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic properties of the test that are **independent of disease prevalence** [2].

**Positive & Negative Predictive Values (PPV, NPV):** The clinical probabilities that a patient with a positive test truly has disease (PPV) or a negative test is truly disease-free (NPV). By **Bayes' theorem**, PPV and NPV depend critically on **disease prevalence**—as prevalence falls, PPV plummets and NPV rises [1][2].

**Likelihood Ratios (LR+, LR−) & ROC Curves:** Likelihood ratios summarize how much a test result shifts pre-test odds to post-test odds independently of prevalence [2]. A **Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve** plots Sensitivity against **1 − Specificity (false-positive rate)** across all possible diagnostic cutoffs; the **Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)** ranges from **0.50** (no better than chance) to **1.00** (perfect discrimination) (e.g., OCT RNFL AUC ~0.88–0.94 vs. single IOP >21 mmHg AUC ~0.65) [1][2].

sections.heading: 2. False Positive & False Negative Diagnoses: Individual and Societal Significance

blocks.text: Because the prevalence of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) in unselected adults over age 40 is relatively low (**~1.5–3%**), Bayes' theorem dictates that even a screening test with **90% sensitivity and 90% specificity** produces **more than five false positives for every true positive** (PPV = 15.5% in a population of 10,000, as illustrated in Figure 1A) [1][2]. Consequently, balancing false positives against false negatives carries profound consequences at both individual and public-health levels [1][2].

rows: Severe psychological anxiety (**"labeling effect"**); exposure to unnecessary lifelong eye drops with local/systemic adverse effects (hyperemia, bronchospasm, bradycardia); out-of-pocket financial cost; lost workdays and insurance/licensing barriers [1][2]

**Overwhelming of specialty glaucoma clinics** and diagnostic resources (OCT/perimetry backlogs delaying care for truly severe patients); enormous wasted healthcare expenditure; erosion of public confidence in screening programs [1][2]

**False reassurance** delaying presentation until advanced, irreversible optic nerve injury and visual field loss occur; loss of reading/driving independence, increased risk of falls, depression, and reduced quality of life [1][2]

Escalating **societal economic burden of preventable blindness** (low-vision rehabilitation, caregiver costs, loss of productive workforce years); increased disability claims and potential **medicolegal liability** [1][2]

sections.heading: 3. Case-Based (Opportunistic) vs. Community-Based (Population) Screening

blocks.text: Evaluating screening strategies against the **Wilson–Jungner criteria** explains why international bodies (World Glaucoma Association [WGA] and USPSTF) currently **do not endorse unselected mass population screening** for POAG, favoring **opportunistic case-finding** and targeted high-risk screening instead [1][2].

rows: Asymptomatic general public recruited outside clinics (community camps, mobile vans, workplaces) [1][2]
Patients already presenting to eye-care clinics for unrelated complaints (presbyopia, cataract, dry eye) [1][2]
Low baseline prevalence (~1–3%) → **very low PPV** and high false-positive referral burden unless specificity exceeds ~98% [1][2]
Higher enriched pre-test probability (older age, risk factors) → **substantially higher PPV** and diagnostic efficiency [1][2]
Relies on portable rapid tools (tonometry alone misses ~40–50% of POAG/NTG); high total program cost per true case detected [1][2]
Immediate access to **comprehensive multimodal exam** (Goldmann applanation, gonioscopy, stereoscopic ONH, OCT, perimetry) at low incremental cost [1][2]
Poor referral completion (often <50% attend tertiary confirmatory visits) and poor long-term adherence [2]
Direct, immediate diagnosis, counseling, treatment initiation, and continuity of care within the clinic [1][2]
Cost-effective **only if targeted to high-risk cohorts** (age >50, African/Hispanic/South Asian ancestry, positive family history) using combined structure + function testing [1][2]
**Recommended gold-standard strategy** globally for glaucoma case detection [1][2]

sections.heading: 4. Number Needed to Treat (NNT), t-Tests & Life-Table (Survival) Analysis

blocks.text: A. Number Needed to Treat (NNT)

**Number Needed to Treat (NNT)** is an intuitive clinical measure of treatment magnitude representing the average number of patients who must receive an intervention over a defined time period to prevent **one additional adverse event** compared with a control group [2][3]. It is the reciprocal of the **Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR)** (whereas **Number Needed to Harm [NNH]** equals the reciprocal of Absolute Risk Increase) [2][4].

ARR = Control Event Rate (CER) − Experimental Event Rate (EER)
NNT = 1 / ARR   (rounded up to nearest whole integer; specify time horizon)

blocks.title: Landmark Glaucoma NNT Examples
items: **Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS):** Five-year conversion from OHT to POAG was **9.5%** in the observation arm versus **4.4%** in the treated arm (ARR = 5.1%), yielding an overall **5-year NNT ≈ 20** [3]. When stratified by baseline risk, the highest-risk tertile had an **NNT ≈ 7**, whereas the lowest-risk tertile had an **NNT ≈ 98**—proving the clinical value of risk-stratified therapy [3].
**Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial (EMGT):** Six-year progression occurred in **62%** of untreated controls versus **45%** of treated POAG patients (ARR = 17%), corresponding to an **NNT ≈ 6** [3].

blocks.text: B. Student's t-Tests

The **Student's t-test** is a parametric statistical hypothesis test used to compare the **means of continuous, approximately normally distributed variables** (such as IOP in mmHg, CCT in µm, or visual field Mean Deviation in dB) when the population standard deviation is unknown [2][4]. Three major forms are used in ophthalmic research [4]:

items: **One-Sample t-Test:** Compares the mean of a single sample against a known theoretical or population reference mean (e.g., comparing mean CCT of a clinic cohort against 540 µm) [4].

**Unpaired (Independent Two-Sample) t-Test:** Compares means between **two mutually independent groups** (e.g., mean 12-month IOP reduction with latanoprost versus timolol in parallel randomized arms) [4].

**Paired (Dependent) t-Test:** Compares two correlated measurements obtained from the **same individuals or matched fellow eyes** (e.g., baseline IOP versus 6-month post-SLT IOP in the same eyes); by removing between-subject variance, it provides higher statistical power [4].

blocks.text: Key statistical caveats include verifying normality (otherwise using non-parametric equivalents: **Mann–Whitney U test** for unpaired and **Wilcoxon signed-rank test** for paired data), using **ANOVA** rather than multiple t-tests when comparing ≥3 groups (to prevent inflation of **Type I error [α, false-positive rate, conventionally 0.05]**), and ensuring adequate sample size to minimize **Type II error (β, false-negative rate; Statistical Power = 1 − β, conventionally ≥80%)** [2][4].
C. Life-Table (Survival) Analysis

**Life-table (survival) analysis** analyzes **time-to-event data** (such as time to surgical failure in the TVT/PTVT trials or time to visual field progression in OHTS/EMGT) over variable follow-up durations [2][4]. Its decisive advantage over simple proportions is proper statistical handling of **right-censored observations**—patients who are lost to follow-up, die, or reach the end of the study without experiencing the event still contribute valid exposure time until their last known visit [2][4].

items: **Actuarial (Cutler–Ederer) Life-Table Method:** Aggregates follow-up into fixed predefined intervals (e.g., 6-month or 1-year intervals), assuming censored subjects were at risk for half the interval [2][4].

**Kaplan–Meier (Product-Limit) Method:** Recalculates cumulative survival probability at the **exact time of each failure event**, generating a crisp step-function curve; it is the gold standard in modern glaucoma surgical and clinical trials [2][4].

**Curve Comparison & Multivariable Modeling:** Differences between two or more Kaplan–Meier curves are tested using the non-parametric **Log-Rank test**, while **Cox Proportional Hazards Regression** estimates adjusted **Hazard Ratios (HR)** accounting for multiple covariates (e.g., age, baseline IOP, CCT) [2][4].

sections.heading: 5. Prospective vs. Retrospective Studies, Case-Control & Cohort Studies

blocks.text: In **prospective studies**, investigators define standardized protocols and enroll participants *before* outcomes occur, following them forward in time; this minimizes recall and measurement bias and establishes temporal sequence, at the expense of higher cost, long duration, and attrition [2][4]. In **retrospective studies**, both exposure and outcome have already occurred prior to study initiation (e.g., chart reviews or registry lookups); they are faster, less expensive, and well suited for rare diseases or long latency periods, but are vulnerable to incomplete medical records, selection bias, recall bias, and unmeasured confounding [2][4].

rows: Starts with **outcome** (glaucoma cases vs. matched disease-free controls) and looks **backward** for prior exposures [4]
**Odds Ratio (OR)** (approximates RR when disease is rare; cannot compute true incidence) [4]

Fast, inexpensive, ideal for rare glaucomas (e.g., ICE syndrome, *LOXL1* PXF genetics) and multiple risk factors; susceptible to **recall bias, selection bias (Berkson bias)**, and reverse causality [2][4]
Starts with **exposure status** (exposed vs. unexposed, disease-free at baseline) and follows **forward** for incident outcomes [4]
**Relative Risk (RR)**, Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR), or **Hazard Ratio (HR)** [4]

Establishes temporality, directly measures true **incidence**, and evaluates multiple outcomes from one exposure; expensive and prone to **loss to follow-up** (Ex: **Barbados Incidence Study**, **Rotterdam Study**) [2][4]
Assesses exposure and disease **simultaneously** at a single point in time [4]
Measures community disease burden and screening yields; cannot establish causality (Ex: **Baltimore Eye Survey**, **APEDS**, **Chennai Glaucoma Study**) [1][4]
Randomly allocates participants to intervention vs. control and follows prospectively [4]

**Gold standard for causality**—randomization balances both known and unknown confounders; high cost and strict inclusion criteria may limit generalizability (Ex: **OHTS, EMGT, CNTGS, TVT, LiGHT**) [3][4]

mcqs.q: A community screening program for POAG (true population prevalence 2%) uses a test with 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity in 10,000 adults. What is the approximate Positive Predictive Value (PPV) of this test?
mcqs.explanation: Among 10,000 people with 2% prevalence (200 diseased, 9,800 healthy), 90% sensitivity yields 180 TP and 90% specificity yields 980 FP. Thus PPV = TP / (TP + FP) = 180 / (180 + 980) = 15.5%, illustrating why mass screening yields excessive false positives.

sections.heading: 1. Traumatic Glaucoma & Angle Recession Glaucoma

blocks.text: **Traumatic glaucoma** encompasses a spectrum of early and late secondary glaucomas following closed-globe blunt trauma, open-globe penetrating injury, or chemical (especially alkali) burns [1][2]. In blunt injury, rapid anteroposterior corneal indentation drives compensatory equatorial scleral expansion and a hydraulic shock wave across the anterior segment, disrupting up to seven circular tissue rings—including the trabecular meshwork, ciliary body face, iris sphincter/root, and lens zonules [1][2].
A. Early Post-Traumatic Mechanisms (<1 Month)

items: **Hyphema & Sickle Cell Hemoglobinopathy:** Fresh erythrocytes, platelets, and fibrin physically obstruct the trabecular meshwork; patients with **sickle cell trait or disease** face catastrophic IOP spikes and optic nerve infarction even with small hyphemas because rigid, sickled red cells cannot traverse the meshwork (contraindicating carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and hyperosmotics that promote hemoconcentration and anterior chamber acidosis) [1][2].

**Ghost Cell Glaucoma:** Develops **2–4 weeks** after vitreous hemorrhage when the anterior hyaloid face is disrupted (trauma, vitrectomy, cataract surgery); degenerated, hemoglobin-depleted erythrocytes (**ghost cells** containing Heinz bodies) become spherical, **khaki-colored, and rigid**, migrating anteriorly to obstruct the trabecular meshwork [1][2].

**Hemolytic & Hemosiderotic Glaucoma:** Hemoglobin-laden macrophages clog the trabecular meshwork (**hemolytic**, weeks post-bleed), whereas retained chronic intraocular iron from blood or a metallic foreign body causes direct **hemosiderotic** trabecular endothelial toxicity months to years later [2].

**Direct Trabecular Contusion, Traumatic Uveitis & Lens Displacement:** Immediate trabecular edema/tears, inflammatory plasmoid aqueous, or zonular rupture causing phacomorphic/pupillary block [1][2].

blocks.text: B. Late Angle Recession Glaucoma

**Angle recession** is a post-traumatic tear into the anterior face of the ciliary body **between the longitudinal and circular ciliary muscle fibers** [1][2]. Although the initial cleft itself does not cause chronic IOP elevation, concomitant trabecular damage stimulates progressive fibrotic scarring and proliferation of a **Descemet-like hyaline membrane** across the inner trabecular meshwork surface, resulting in **late-onset secondary open-angle glaucoma** with bimodal peaks within the first year and **10 or more years** post-injury [1][2].

The risk of glaucoma correlates directly with the circumferential extent of recession: eyes with **>180° of angle recession** carry a **6–10% lifetime incidence** (rising steeply above 240°–270°) [1][2]. Because up to 50% of uninjured fellow eyes eventually exhibit POAG or steroid responsiveness, angle recession may unmask an underlying genetic predisposition [2]. **Bilateral comparison gonioscopy** is diagnostic, showing a **markedly widened, irregular ciliary body band**, a glistening prominent white scleral spur, torn iris processes, hyperpigmentation, and localized PAS—often accompanied by a Vossius ring, sphincter tears, iridodialysis, or phacodonesis [1][2].

sections.heading: 2. Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG)

blocks.text: **Neovascular glaucoma** is a devastating, refractory secondary glaucoma caused by anterior segment neovascularization driven by severe **posterior segment retinal ischemia** in ~97% of cases [1][2]. The three leading etiologies are **proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR, ~33%)**, **ischemic central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO, ~33%—classically "90-day glaucoma")**, and **ocular ischemic syndrome / carotid artery occlusive disease (~13%)**; less frequent causes include CRAO, BRVO, chronic retinal detachment, radiation retinopathy, uveal melanoma, and chronic uveitis [1][2].

**Pathophysiology:** Retinal capillary non-perfusion stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), triggering massive secretion of **vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)** (along with IL-6, bFGF, and PDGF) [1][2]. VEGF diffuses forward into the anterior chamber—greatly accelerated after **pars plana vitrectomy or posterior capsulotomy**, which eliminate the lens/vitreous diffusion barrier—stimulating abnormal **neovascularization of the iris (NVI)** and **angle (NVA)** embedded within a contractile **myofibroblastic fibrovascular membrane** [1][2].

items: **Stage 1 — Pre-Glaucoma (Rubeosis Iridis):** Fine, irregular capillary tufts appear at the pupillary margin (and in ~10% of CRVO eyes, NVA precedes NVI—making **undilated gonioscopy mandatory** in all ischemic retinas); IOP remains normal [1][2].

**Stage 2 — Secondary Open-Angle Glaucoma:** A translucent fibrovascular membrane proliferates across the trabecular meshwork despite an anatomically open angle, obstructing conventional outflow and causing elevated IOP, anterior chamber flare, and spontaneous hyphema [1][2].

**Stage 3 — Secondary Synechial Angle-Closure Glaucoma:** Contraction of myofibroblasts within the fibrovascular membrane pulls the peripheral iris anteriorly onto the trabecular meshwork (**"zippering" the angle closed**), culminating in **360° broad PAS**, **ectropion uveae**, fixed dilated pupil, corneal edema, severe pain, and fulminant IOP (40–70 mmHg) [1][2].

sections.heading: 3. Iridocorneal Endothelial (ICE) Syndrome

blocks.text: **ICE syndrome** is an acquired, **unilateral**, sporadic proliferative corneal endotheliopathy affecting predominantly **middle-aged women (ages 20–50 years)**, hypothesized to be triggered by low-grade viral infection (HSV or EBV DNA identified in corneal endothelial specimens) [1][3]. Abnormal corneal endothelial cells undergo **epithelial-like metaplasia** (**ICE cells** expressing cytokeratins, microvilli, and desmosomes) and migrate posteriorly across Schwalbe's line and the trabecular meshwork onto the anterior iris surface, secreting an abnormal basement membrane (**Campbell's membrane**) [1][3].

Progressive contraction of this migrating cellular membrane draws the peripheral iris high across the angle (**broad PAS extending anterior to Schwalbe's line**), displaces the pupil toward the PAS (**corectopia**), stretches and thins the opposite iris stroma into **stretch and melt holes**, and produces refractory secondary angle-closure glaucoma in approximately **50% of patients** [1][3]. On **specular microscopy**, ICE cells display pathognomonic **"dark–light reversal"** (dark cell interiors with bright intercellular borders and a central bright spot), sharply differentiating ICE from **posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (PPCD)** (bilateral, autosomal dominant) and **Axenfeld–Rieger syndrome** (bilateral, congenital) [3].

rows: Predominant **corneal edema** (often at normal or mildly raised IOP) with classic **"beaten-bronze"** corneal endothelium; mild corectopia and minimal iris atrophy [3]
Mild-to-moderate; less frequent than other two variants [3]
Severe progressive **corectopia** (toward PAS), **ectropion uveae**, full-thickness **stretch holes** (opposite quadrant) and **melt holes** (ischemia) [3]
Severe, progressive refractory synechial angle-closure glaucoma [3]

Severe refractory glaucoma; must differentiate from diffuse iris melanoma [3]

sections.heading: 4. Complex Uveitic Glaucoma

blocks.text: **Uveitic glaucoma** exemplifies a notoriously complex secondary glaucoma driven by competing inflammatory and iatrogenic forces across both open-angle and angle-closure pathways [1][2]. Infectious etiologies (**HSV, VZV, and CMV trabeculitis**, tuberculosis, syphilis, toxoplasmosis) and immune-mediated syndromes (**JIA**, **Fuchs uveitis**, **Posner–Schlossman**, **HLA-B27**, **sarcoidosis**, **VKH**, and **Behçet disease**) cause fluctuating IOP—oscillating between ciliary body shutdown (hypotony) and dramatic pressure spikes [1][2].

Pathophysiologically, blood–aqueous barrier disruption introduces plasmoid proteins and inflammatory cells that clog the trabecular meshwork alongside acute trabeculitis, chronic trabecular fibrosis, and **steroid-induced extracellular matrix deposition**; simultaneously, 360° posterior synechiae (**iris bombé**), contracting inflammatory exudates (broad/tent-shaped PAS), or annular ciliochoroidal effusion (VKH) precipitate angle closure [1][2]. Clinically, hallmarks such as **sectoral iris atrophy** (herpetic), **stellate KPs with Amsler angle bleeding** (Fuchs), or a **quiet white eye in a child** (JIA) guide targeted antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and surgical care [2][3].

sections.heading: 5. Multimechanism Glaucoma

blocks.text: **Multimechanism glaucoma** occurs when **two or more independent pathogenic mechanisms** concurrently or sequentially elevate IOP in the same eye [1][4]. Recognizing overlapping mechanisms is essential at fellowship level because treating only a single mechanism—such as performing LPI alone in combined-mechanism disease—leaves residual uncontrolled IOP and progressive optic nerve damage [1][4].

rows: **Primary angle closure** (pupillary block and/or plateau iris) superimposed on intrinsic **open-angle trabecular outflow resistance** (coexistent POAG or subclinical trabecular damage from chronic iridotrabecular contact) [1][4]
IOP remains elevated despite a **patent LPI** and an anatomically open angle on post-laser gonioscopy [1][4]

Open-angle trabecular obstruction by fibrillar PXF material + pigment, compounded by **zonular laxity** allowing forward lens shift → **secondary pupillary block/angle closure** (10–30% of PXF eyes) [1][4]
Markedly asymmetric IOP spikes, Sampaolesi line, phacodonesis, and progressive anterior chamber shallowing [1][4]

1. **Acute pupillary block** (buoyant oil occluding pupil in aphakic/pseudophakic eyes lacking an inferior Ando iridotomy); 2. **Open-angle obstruction** by emulsified oil microdroplets ("inverse hypopyon") and macrophage trabeculitis; 3. **Steroid response**; 4. **Scleral buckle** vortex-vein compression/ciliary congestion; 5. Underlying NVG [2][4]
Glistening hyper-reflective oil bubbles in superior angle on gonioscopy; high IOP early (block/overfill) or late (emulsification/PAS) [2][4]

Mechanical **trabecular collapse/angle distortion** (tight/long sutures, same-size graft), progressive **PAS**, retained **viscoelastic/inflammatory debris**, and chronic **topical corticosteroid response** [2][4]
Leading cause of late graft failure and irreversible vision loss post-PKP; requires careful tonometry (Tono-Pen/iCare) and early GDD [2][4]

1.quote: Angle recession tears between longitudinal and circular ciliary muscle fibers (>180 deg carries 6-10% late glaucoma risk). NVG progresses through rubeosis, open-angle fibrovascular membrane, and synechial closure with ectropion uveae. Combined mechanism involves residual open-angle resistance post-LPI.

2.quote: NVG arises from PDR (33%), ischemic CRVO (33%, '90-day glaucoma'), and OIS (13%). Ghost cell glaucoma occurs 2-4 weeks post-vitreous hemorrhage via rigid khaki-colored degenerated RBCs. Silicone oil and PKP glaucomas exemplify complex multimechanism secondary glaucomas.

3.quote: ICE syndrome is a unilateral sporadic endotheliopathy in middle-aged women with specular 'dark-light reversal' and migrating epithelialized ICE cells (Campbell membrane) causing high PAS above Schwalbe's line across Chandler, Essential Iris Atrophy, and Cogan-Reese variants.

4.quote: Multimechanism glaucoma—including combined PAC/POAG, PXF with zonular-laxity angle closure, post-PKP, and silicone oil glaucoma—requires identifying and addressing every concurrent open-angle, angle-closure, and steroid-related pathway.

mcqs.q: Histopathologically, angle recession following blunt ocular trauma represents a tear at which exact anatomical plane?
options: Separation of the ciliary body band from its attachment at the scleral spur
A longitudinal tear into the ciliary body face between the longitudinal and circular ciliary muscle fibers
Detachment of the iris root from the anterior ciliary body face
Circumferential splitting of Descemet's membrane at Schwalbe's line
mcqs.explanation: Angle recession is a tear between the longitudinal and circular fibers of the ciliary muscle (widening the ciliary body band), whereas separation of the ciliary body from the scleral spur is a cyclodialysis cleft (causing hypotony) and root detachment is iridodialysis.

mcqs.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with unilateral corneal edema ('beaten-bronze' endothelium), mild corectopia, broad PAS extending anterior to Schwalbe's line, and IOP of 30 mmHg. Specular microscopy demonstrates dark intracellular areas with bright intercellular borders ('dark–light reversal'). Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (PPCD)
Axenfeld–Rieger syndrome
Chandler variant of iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome
Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy
mcqs.explanation: Unilateral presentation in a middle-aged woman with beaten-bronze corneal edema, high PAS anterior to Schwalbe's line, and specular 'dark–light reversal' is pathognomonic of the Chandler variant of ICE syndrome (unlike bilateral inherited PPCD or Axenfeld–Rieger).

mcqs.q: Three weeks following traumatic vitreous hemorrhage and ruptured anterior hyaloid face, a patient develops an IOP of 48 mmHg with an open angle and tan-colored cells circulating in the anterior chamber without significant keratic precipitates. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Direct obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by rigid, hemoglobin-depleted degenerated erythrocytes (ghost cells)
Contraction of a VEGF-induced myofibroblastic membrane causing 360° PAS
Late proliferation of a Descemet-like hyaline membrane over a recessed angle
Macrophage ingestion of emulsified silicone oil microdroplets
mcqs.explanation: Ghost cell glaucoma arises 2–4 weeks after vitreous hemorrhage with a disrupted anterior hyaloid face when degenerated, spherical, khaki-colored rigid RBCs containing Heinz bodies migrate anteriorly and obstruct the trabecular meshwork.

advanced-2.shortTitle: Complex Glaucoma Exam, Post-Op Complications & Atypical Fields

sections.heading: 1. Key Specialized Examination Techniques in Complex Glaucoma

blocks.text: Evaluating complicated, postoperative, or refractory glaucomas demands targeted diagnostic modalities that extend far beyond routine Goldmann applanation and 24-2 perimetry [1][2]:

items: **Dynamic Indentation (Four-Mirror) Gonioscopy:** Indispensable to differentiate appositional versus synechial closure, elicit the **"double-hump" sign** of plateau iris, detect subtle **NVA prior to pupillary dilation**, compare contralateral angle width in angle recession, identify **cyclodialysis clefts** or emulsified silicone oil, and inspect internal trabeculectomy ostium patency or tube placement [1][2].

**Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM, 35–50 MHz):** Because high-frequency ultrasound penetrates the pigmented iris epithelium, UBM is the gold standard for retro-iridal pathology—confirming **plateau iris configuration** (anteriorly rotated ciliary processes with obliterated ciliary sulcus), **supraciliary/choroidal effusions**, **aqueous misdirection**, ciliary body cysts/tumors, cyclodialysis clefts, and zonular dialysis [1][2].

**Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT):** Provides rapid, non-contact cross-sectional imaging of angle parameters (AOD500, TISA), internal **filtering bleb wall architecture** (epithelial microcysts, subconjunctival fluid spaces, Tenon cyst encapsulation), corneal endothelial–tube distance, and Descemet membrane detachments [1][2].

**Structured Bleb Grading & Seidel Testing:** Systematic grading via the **Moorfields Bleb Grading System (MBGS)** or **Indiana Bleb Appearance Grading Scale (IBAGS)** tracks bleb area, height, vascularity (corkscrew vessels signaling impending scarring vs. thin avascular cystic walls risking infection), and **Seidel testing** (concentrated 2% fluorescein under cobalt-blue illumination identifying spontaneous or gentle provocative aqueous leakage) [1][2].

**Corneal, Macular & Neuro-Ophthalmic Diagnostics:** **Specular microscopy** guides endothelial safety prior to tube/MIGS surgery or in ICE/post-PKP eyes; **macular GCIPL OCT** and **10-2 automated perimetry** monitor eyes with split fixation or advanced RNFL floor effect; **contrast MRI of brain and orbits** is mandatory whenever atypical disc pallor or vertical-meridian field loss raises suspicion of compressive neuro-ophthalmic disease [1][3].

sections.heading: 2. Postoperative Shallow or Flat Anterior Chamber: Diagnostic & Management Algorithm

blocks.text: A **shallow or flat anterior chamber** following filtering surgery is rapidly stratified using **IOP**, **bleb morphology**, **Seidel status**, **patency of the peripheral iridotomy (PI)**, and **posterior segment / B-scan ultrasonography** [1][2]. Grading chamber depth (**Spaeth Grade I:** peripheral iridocorneal touch; **Grade II:** pupillary border–cornea touch; **Grade III:** **lenticulocorneal touch**—a surgical emergency risking rapid cataract and corneal decompensation) dictates urgency of intervention [2].

blocks.text: High-Yield Postoperative Emergencies

items: **Aqueous Misdirection (Malignant Glaucoma / Ciliary Block):** Characterized by **uniform axial shallowing** (both central and peripheral AC equally shallow), elevated IOP, flat bleb, and a **patent PI**—occurring most often in hyperopic/nanophthalmic angle-closure eyes where anterior hyaloid–ciliary process apposition diverts aqueous posteriorly into the vitreous [1][2]. Stepwise therapy begins with intensive **cycloplegics** (atropine 1% + phenylephrine), aqueous suppressants, and IV **mannitol**; if refractory, perform **Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy/anterior hyaloidotomy** (in pseudophakes/aphakes) or definitive **pars plana vitrectomy with irido-zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy (IZHV)** to establish an unobstructed unicameral eye [1][2].

**Delayed Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage (SCH):** Presents days postoperatively (risk factors: high preoperative IOP, aphakia, anticoagulation, hypertension, hypotony, Valsalva) with sudden **excruciating pain**, rock-hard IOP, and dark brown **non-transilluminating choroidal domes** (B-scan reveals bright heterogeneous choroidal echoes) [2]. Immediate management comprises wound closure, IOP/BP control, steroids, and analgesia; surgical **sclerotomy drainage is optimally delayed 7–14 days** until serial B-scans confirm clot liquefaction, unless intractable pain, corneal touch, or retinal kissing mandates earlier drainage [2].

sections.heading: 3. Management of Complicated Medical & Surgical Glaucoma Scenarios

blocks.text: A. Bleb Complications: Failing, Encapsulated & Infected Blebs

items: **Early Failing Bleb:** Intensify topical corticosteroids, apply gentle digital ocular compression, perform **laser suture lysis** (within 2–4 weeks; later after MMC) or remove releasable sutures, and proceed to **slit-lamp bleb needling with subconjunctival 5-FU or MMC** when episcleral fibrosis persists [1][2].

**Encapsulated Bleb (Tenon's Cyst):** Tense, elevated, dome-shaped, hyperemic bleb developing at 2–6 weeks; initiate conservative aqueous suppressants and topical steroids (many remodel spontaneously), performing **needling with 5-FU/MMC** if IOP remains uncontrolled [2].

**Blebitis vs. Bleb-Associated Endophthalmitis (BAE):** Thin avascular MMC blebs (especially inferiorly placed or leaking) risk late infection by *Streptococcus*, *Haemophilus*, or *Staphylococcus* [2]. Isolated **blebitis** (milky bleb without vitritis) is treated aggressively with hourly fortified topical antibiotics (vancomycin + ceftazidime/fluoroquinolone); **BAE** (hypopyon + vitritis) demands emergency **vitreous tap/biopsy + intravitreal vancomycin (1 mg/0.1 mL) and ceftazidime (2.25 mg/0.1 mL)** (plus pars plana vitrectomy for severe/LP vision) [2].

blocks.text: B. Glaucoma Drainage Device (GDD) Complications & Landmark Trial Evidence

Managing GDDs requires vigilance for the **hypertensive phase** (4–8 weeks post-Ahmed valve; treated early with aqueous suppressants), **tube/plate erosion** (an endophthalmitis emergency requiring donor scleral, pericardial, or corneal patch grafting and conjunctival closure), **corneal endothelial cell loss** (managed by trimming or repositioning the tube into the **ciliary sulcus or pars plana**), and restrictive **strabismus/diplopia** [2]. Evidence from landmark surgical trials guides procedure selection [4]:

blocks.title: Landmark Surgical Trials in Complex Glaucoma
items: **Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (TVT, 5-Year):** In eyes with prior cataract or failed trabeculectomy surgery, Baerveldt 350 mm² GDD achieved a lower cumulative failure rate (**29.8%**) than MMC trabeculectomy (**46.9%**) with fewer early complications and similar 5-year mean IOP (~14 mmHg) [4].

**Primary Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (PTVT, 5-Year):** In eyes *without* prior incisional surgery, failure rates were similar at 5 years (42% tube vs. 35% trabeculectomy), but primary trabeculectomy achieved lower IOP on fewer medications [4].

**ABC & AVB Trials (5-Year Pooled):** Baerveldt achieved lower mean IOP and lower failure rates than the valved Ahmed FP7 implant, at the expense of higher **persistent hypotony** (~4–5% vs. ~0–1%)—supporting valved AGV in eyes prone to hypotony (e.g., uveitis, NVG) and non-valved Baerveldt/AADI when very low target IOP is needed [4].

blocks.text: C. Complex Secondary Open-Angle & Angle-Closure Management

items: **Neovascular Glaucoma:** Urgent **intravitreal anti-VEGF** (regresses NVI/NVA within 48–72 hours) + definitive **panretinal photocoagulation (PRP)** + aqueous suppressants/atropine + **GDD (valved AGV preferred acutely)** or MMC trabeculectomy once quiescent; TSCPC for non-seeing painful eyes [1][2].

**ICE Syndrome, Post-PKP & Silicone Oil:** In ICE and post-PKP eyes, **GDDs** (with sulcus/pars plana tube placement to protect corneal grafts) outperform trabeculectomy, whose ostium frequently occludes with migrating ICE membrane [1][2]. In aphakic/pseudophakic **silicone oil** eyes, perform an **inferior Ando surgical iridotomy** to prevent oil-induced pupillary block, followed by early oil removal and GDD or cyclophotocoagulation if IOP remains elevated [2].

**Persistent Angle Closure Post-LPI & Nanophthalmos:** Treat **plateau iris syndrome** with **argon laser peripheral iridoplasty (ALPI)**, low-dose pilocarpine, or clear lens extraction [1][2]. In **nanophthalmos** (axial length <20 mm, thickened sclera blocking vortex venous outflow), mitigate catastrophic intraoperative uveal effusion by performing prophylactic **partial-thickness lamellar sclerectomies** during intraocular surgery [2].

Frequently missed on 24-2 (6° grid); mandatory **10-2 perimetry (2° grid)** and macular GCIPL OCT. Carries ~0.5–2% risk of unexplained postoperative central vision loss (**"wipe-out" / snuff-out**)—avoid perioperative hypotony and retrobulbar volume spikes [1][2]
Focal injury to **nasal radiating RNFL fibers** (<3% of glaucomatous fields) [1][3]
Originates at the blind spot extending temporally; **does not respect the horizontal meridian** [1][3]
**Double Arcuate Ring Scotoma with Temporal Island** [1][3]
Confluence of superior and inferior arcuate scotomas in **end-stage glaucoma** (sparing central 5° and peripheral temporal crescent) [1][3]
Differentiate from **retinitis pigmentosa**, extensive panretinal photocoagulation, and vigabatrin toxicity; monitor residual central island with **10-2 size III or V** stimulus [1][3]
Strictly respects the **vertical meridian** → **chiasmal** (pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, meningioma) or **post-chiasmal** (stroke, tumor) lesion [3]

**Neuro-ophthalmic RED FLAG** masquerading as NTG! Correlate with neuroretinal rim **pallor disproportionate to cupping**, age <50, rapid unilateral drop, or dyschromatopsia → **urgent contrast MRI brain/orbits** [1][3]
Cecocentral = **papillomacular bundle** (toxic/nutritional, ethambutol, LHON, compressive); Altitudinal = **NAION / arteritic AION** or BRVO [3]
Promptly evaluate ESR/CRP (giant cell arteritis), B₁₂/folate, medication history, and genetic/neuro-ophthalmic workup rather than escalating glaucoma drops [3]

Binasal: bilateral dense glaucomatous nasal steps, optic disc drusen, or dolichoectatic internal carotid arteries; Tilted disc: inferonasal myopic staphyloma causing **superotemporal depression crossing midline** [3]

Tilted disc defects **improve on repeat perimetry with added minus sphere**; always rule out **lens-rim artifact**, **ptosis**, and **cloverleaf inattention pattern** before diagnosing progression [1][3]

1.chapter: Clinical Evaluation, Perimetry & Surgical Complications in Complex Glaucoma
1.quote: Dynamic indentation gonioscopy, UBM, AS-OCT, 10-2 perimetry, and macular GCIPL OCT are essential in complex glaucoma. Aqueous misdirection shows axial shallowing with patent PI and high IOP; split-fixation eyes carry postoperative wipe-out risk.

2.book: Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma (7th Edition) — Allingham et al.
2.chapter: Chapters 33–36: Complications of Filtering Surgery, Drainage Implants & Refractory Glaucomas
2.quote: Stratify shallow AC by IOP (low: bleb leak, overfiltration, choroidal effusion; high: pupillary block, aqueous misdirection, suprachoroidal hemorrhage). Delay SCH drainage 7-14 days for liquefaction on B-scan. Bleb-associated endophthalmitis requires urgent vitreous tap and intravitreal vancomycin + ceftazidime.

3.book: AAO BCSC Section 5: Neuro-Ophthalmology & Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology (9th Ed.)
3.chapter: Visual Field Interpretation & Neuro-Ophthalmic Masqueraders of Glaucoma
3.quote: Defects respecting the vertical meridian (bitemporal or homonymous hemianopia), cecocentral scotomas, and rim pallor out of proportion to cupping mandate urgent MRI brain/orbits. Temporal wedge defects (<3%) arise from nasal RNFL loss; tilted disc defects cross midline and improve with minus lens.

4.book: Gedde SJ et al. (TVT 5-yr, AJO 2012; PTVT 5-yr, Ophthalmology 2022) & Budenz DL / Christakis PG (ABC/AVB 5-yr)
4.quote: TVT 5-year failure was 29.8% for Baerveldt tube vs 46.9% for MMC trabeculectomy in previously operated eyes. PTVT favored primary trabeculectomy for medication burden. Pooled ABC/AVB showed lower IOP with Baerveldt but lower hypotony risk with valved Ahmed FP7.

mcqs.q: Two days after trabeculectomy in a hyperopic eye with primary angle-closure glaucoma, the patient develops an IOP of 42 mmHg, a flat filtering bleb, a patent peripheral iridotomy, and uniform axial shallowing of both central and peripheral anterior chamber. After medical therapy and Nd:YAG hyaloidotomy fail, what is the definitive surgical procedure?
options: Immediate sclerotomy drainage of the suprachoroidal space
Transconjunctival scleral flap compression sutures with viscoelastic reformation
Argon laser peripheral iridoplasty (ALPI)
Pars plana vitrectomy with irido-zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy (IZHV) to create a unicameral eye
mcqs.explanation: Uniform axial shallowing (central and peripheral AC) with elevated IOP, flat bleb, and patent PI is diagnostic of aqueous misdirection (malignant glaucoma). Definitive surgical cure requires pars plana vitrectomy with irido-zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy (IZHV) establishing free communication from vitreous to AC.

mcqs.q: A 46-year-old patient referred as 'normal-tension glaucoma' (IOP 15 mmHg OU) shows temporal neuroretinal rim pallor disproportionate to cupping and a bilateral visual field defect sharply respecting the vertical meridian. What is the single most appropriate next step?
options: Start evening latanoprost and repeat 24-2 perimetry in 6 months
Order urgent contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and orbits to rule out a chiasmal or intracranial compressive lesion
Perform bilateral Nd:YAG laser peripheral iridotomy
Repeat automated perimetry with a +3.00 D near add to correct for tilted disc
mcqs.explanation: Visual field defects strictly respecting the vertical meridian (bitemporal or homonymous hemianopia) combined with rim pallor disproportionate to cupping and young age are critical neuro-ophthalmic red flags requiring urgent contrast MRI brain/orbits.

mcqs.q: According to the 5-year results of the Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (TVT) Study in eyes with prior cataract or failed glaucoma surgery, how did the Baerveldt 350 mm² implant compare with trabeculectomy with mitomycin C?
options: Baerveldt tube shunt had a significantly lower 5-year cumulative failure rate (29.8% vs 46.9%) with similar mean IOP (~14 mmHg)
Trabeculectomy had a significantly lower 5-year cumulative failure rate (29.8% vs 46.9%)
Baerveldt tube shunt produced markedly higher rates of late bleb-associated endophthalmitis
Both procedures had >80% failure rates by 3 years requiring cyclophotocoagulation
mcqs.explanation: In the 5-year TVT Study of previously operated eyes, the Baerveldt 350 mm² tube shunt achieved a significantly lower cumulative probability of failure (29.8%) than trabeculectomy with MMC (46.9%), with similar mean IOP (~14 mmHg) at 5 years.
